title: Victoria Sponge
subtitle: two light butter sponges sandwiched with jam and cream
excerpt: The Victoria sponge is the benchmark British cake. Light, even, and without fuss. The equal-weight method -- the same weight of butter, sugar, eggs, and flour -- makes it simple to scale and consistent every time. Sandwich with raspberry jam and whipped cream.
sourceNotes: Named after Queen Victoria, who was known to enjoy a slice of sponge cake with her afternoon tea.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the plain sponge layers, unfilled. Fill on the day of serving.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Bake the layers a day ahead. Store in an airtight tin and fill before serving.

content.text: The all-in-one method works well here -- everything goes in the bowl together and is beaten until smooth. The butter must be very soft, not melted. If your eggs are cold from the fridge, bring them to room temperature first or the batter may curdle.
Heat the oven to 180C. Grease two 20cm sandwich tins and line the bases with baking paper.
Put the flour, baking powder, caster sugar, softened butter, eggs, milk, and vanilla into a large bowl. Beat with an electric whisk for 2 minutes until light and smooth.
Divide evenly between the two tins. Smooth the tops. Bake for 22 to 25 minutes until risen, golden, and springing back when pressed.
Cool in the tins for 5 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack. Leave to cool completely before filling.
Spread the jam over the flat side of one layer. Spoon the whipped cream on top. Sandwich with the second layer. Dust the top with a little caster sugar.

items.cause: Under-baked, or oven door opened too early.
items.fix: Do not open the oven door in the first 20 minutes. The cake is done when it springs back cleanly when pressed.

items.cause: Butter or eggs were too cold.
items.fix: Make sure the butter is properly soft before starting. Bring eggs out of the fridge an hour ahead.

content.text: The Victoria sponge is the cake at the centre of British baking culture. It appears at every village fete, bake sale, and birthday. It is the first cake most British home bakers learn to make and the one that everything else is measured against. Simple and as good as it ever was.
